# AI R&D benchmarks in closed-lab model cards {.appendix}

The three closed frontier labs publish, with each frontier release, a system or model card whose
dangerous-capability section reports how far the model is from automating AI research. This
appendix collects those AI R&D scores, one table per lab, with the lab's successive frontier
models as columns and the benchmarks as rows. It is a reference for the cross-lab discussion of
returns to research effort, not a chapter: the runs behind these numbers are not public.

The long-form data with a source and a confidence flag on every row is `data/ai_rd_benchmarks.csv`.
Provenance marks in the cells: no mark means the number was read from the card itself (or from the
METR report the card cites); **\*** means it was read from the lab's launch post because the card
does not give it; **†** means it was read from a search-result excerpt of a write-up and not found
in any primary document; **‡** means it was recalled from memory and not checked. Almost every cell
was verified against the card on 2026-09-13; the handful still marked † or ‡ are launch-blog
figures (SWE-bench Verified for the Codex models, Terminal-Bench for OpenAI models) that no card
contains. Where a later card re-runs an earlier model and gets a different number, the cell keeps
the model's own card value and the notes column records the re-run.

Scores are as the lab reports them and are not comparable across labs: each lab uses its own
scaffold, time budget, attempt count and problem subset, and internal suites are only defined
inside one lab. Conditions that change the number are given in parentheses inside the cell.

The figures are built for reading saturation. Every bounded metric is drawn on its full range with
the ceiling as a solid line; a human reference point stated by the card (an expert solution, a
threshold the card expresses in human-hours) is a red dotted line; a rule-out threshold not tied to
human performance is a grey dashed line. A black cross marks the card at which the lab stopped
reporting a series, whether because it was retired as saturated, replaced by a harder version, or
dropped from the determination. Each lab then gets one overview panel with all of its bounded
evaluations on the same 0 to 100 percent axis, so the order in which benchmarks saturate and get
replaced is visible. Ceilings, directions and reference values are in
`data/ai_rd_benchmark_series.csv`; unbounded metrics (speedups, human-normalized scores above 1,
time horizons) and lower-is-better metrics stay out of the overview.

```{python}
#| echo: false
from src.chapter import *  # noqa
from src import benchmarks
from IPython.display import Markdown, display

def show(lab, families=None, caption=""):
    df = benchmarks.load(lab, frontier_only=True)
    if families:
        df = df[df["family"].isin(families)]
    if df.empty:
        display(Markdown("_No rows recorded._")); return
    t = benchmarks.wide(df)
    display(Markdown(benchmarks.to_markdown(t) + (f"\n\n: {caption}" if caption else "")))

def show_series(lab):
    fig = benchmarks.timeseries(benchmarks.load(lab, frontier_only=True), lab=lab)
    plt.show()

def show_overview(lab):
    fig = benchmarks.overview(benchmarks.load(lab, frontier_only=True), lab)
    plt.show()

def show_cards(lab):
    t = benchmarks.cards(benchmarks.load(lab, frontier_only=True))
    t["card"] = t.apply(lambda r: f"[{r['card_title']}]({r['card_url']})" if r["card_url"] else r["card_title"], axis=1)
    display(Markdown(benchmarks.to_markdown(t[["model", "card_date", "card"]].set_index("model").rename_axis("Model"))))
```

## Google DeepMind

DeepMind's Frontier Safety Framework has a Machine Learning R&D critical capability level. Through
Gemini 3.1 Pro it was evaluated on five of METR's seven RE-Bench tasks, reported as a human-normalized
average within a 32-hour budget; the Gemini 3.7 Flash FSF report switches to an internal research
engineering benchmark (GRB, 74 tasks, 2-hour timeout) with a 90 percent pass@1 rule-out threshold.
Flash cards defer the determination to the most capable Pro model of the time.

::: {.benchmarks .column-screen-inset}

```{python}
show("gdm", caption="Google DeepMind: AI R&D and agentic-coding scores by model card. {#tbl-gdm}")
```

:::

```{python}
show_cards("gdm")
```

```{python}
#| fig-cap: "Google DeepMind: every bounded evaluation on one 0 to 100 percent axis. Colour is the benchmark category; the label at each line's end names the benchmark; a black cross is the card at which the series stops being reported."
show_overview("gdm")
```

```{python}
#| fig-cap: "Google DeepMind: numeric scores over card date, one panel per benchmark series. Bounded metrics show their full range with the ceiling as a solid line; red dotted is a human reference stated by the card, grey dashed a rule-out threshold. Filled points are read from the card; light-filled points are unverified; hollow points are the same model under a different condition."
show_series("gdm")
```

## OpenAI

OpenAI's Preparedness Framework tracks "AI Self-improvement" (earlier "Model autonomy") with a
mix of public and internal evaluations: SWE-bench Verified on a 477-problem subset, SWE-Lancer,
internal pull-request replication (OpenAI PRs), MLE-bench (full set with pass@10 in the o1 era, a
30-competition subset with pass@1 from mid-2025, a revised 72-problem set from GPT-5.6), PaperBench,
research-engineer interview questions, OpenAI-Proof Q&A, an internal research debugging eval and
Monorepo-Bench. The High threshold is worded as "a performant mid-career research engineer".

::: {.benchmarks .column-screen-inset}

```{python}
show("openai", caption="OpenAI: AI self-improvement and agentic-coding scores by system card. {#tbl-openai}")
```

:::

```{python}
show_cards("openai")
```

```{python}
#| fig-cap: "OpenAI: every bounded evaluation on one 0 to 100 percent axis. The research-engineer coding interview saturated first (retired after ChatGPT agent); MLE-bench was revised once the 30-competition subset climbed; OpenAI-Proof Q&A stays near the floor."
show_overview("openai")
```

```{python}
#| fig-cap: "OpenAI: numeric scores over card date. Same marks as above. MLE-bench appears twice because the o1-era cards used the full competition set and pass@10, later cards a 30-competition subset."
show_series("openai")
```

## Anthropic

Anthropic's Responsible Scaling Policy defines AI R&D capability thresholds (AI R&D-4 through Opus
4.6, an "automated AI R&D" threshold from Mythos Preview on) and reports SWE-bench Verified plus a
hard subset used as an RSP checkpoint, two internal AI research evaluation suites with thresholds
stated in human-expert hours, a subset of METR's RE-Bench, staff surveys, and from 2026 an internal
acceleration measure built on a fork of Epoch's Capabilities Index. From Opus 4.8 the card says the
task suites are no longer load-bearing for the determination.

::: {.benchmarks .column-screen-inset}

```{python}
show("anthropic", caption="Anthropic: AI R&D and agentic-coding scores by system card. {#tbl-anthropic}")
```

:::

```{python}
show_cards("anthropic")
```

```{python}
#| fig-cap: "Anthropic: every bounded evaluation on one 0 to 100 percent axis. Text-based RL and SWE-bench Verified approach the ceiling; the novel compiler's complex tests and Suite 2 do not, and from Opus 4.8 the card stops treating the task suites as load-bearing."
show_overview("anthropic")
```

```{python}
#| fig-cap: "Anthropic: numeric scores over card date. Same marks as above. Terminal-Bench is split by version; the Suite 1 speedups use a log axis."
```

## Reading across the three

Each lab measures a different thing under the AI R&D heading. DeepMind reports a single
human-normalized number on a public METR suite; OpenAI reports pass rates on internal replication
tasks and Kaggle-style competitions; Anthropic reports fractions of a human baseline on internal
tasks plus its own RE-Bench subset. SWE-bench Verified is the only benchmark all three report, and
even there the subset and scaffold differ. The common thread is qualitative: every lab has moved
from "well below human" statements in 2024 to reporting models at or above the human baseline on
several-hour ML engineering tasks by 2026, while each still judges the model below its own
threshold for autonomous AI R&D. Two things to watch when reading across cards: benchmark versions
and subsets change (Terminal-Bench 1 to 2.0, 2.1 and 4.0; MLE-bench full to 30 to revised; RE-Bench
7 tasks to 5), and later cards re-run earlier models and print different numbers, so a single
model's score can differ between its own card and a successor's comparison table.
